The ban is a stopgap measure that must be reviewed as crime prevention and management systems improve. After a certain number of years, if individual review or other methods show a person is not especially dangerous to passengers, the restriction should be lifted.

who: People convicted of the listed crimes who want to be taxi drivers
Taxi drivers and the taxi industry

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Service Performance Evaluation Act is unconstitutional because it sets no time limit for the government to impose dismissal as a punishment. The court found that dismissal under that Act is in substance a disciplinary sanction that limits a person's right to hold public office. Having no time limit conflicts with the Constitution's protection of that right, so the time limits in the Civil Servant Discipline Act should be applied by analogy.
raw.held: Dismissal punishments imposed under Article 12, paragraph 1, item 2 of the Act as amended on 28 December 1990 are in substance disciplinary sanctions, and the lack of a time limit for imposing them is contrary to the Constitution's protection. Until the law is fixed, the time limits in the Civil Servant Discipline Act apply by analogy.

points.text: Article 18 of the Constitution protects the right to hold public office, and the state must set up rules for it. Punishing misconduct is allowed, but leaving a civil servant's case uncertain for a long time harms legal stability and fairness.

So if the power to discipline is not used within a reasonable time, the matter should not be pursued any more. This protects civil servants' rights and keeps the legal order stable, and the Civil Servant Discipline Act's ten-year rule follows this idea.
A dismissal punishment under the Performance Evaluation Act limits the right to hold public office, so it is in substance a disciplinary sanction.

Because that Act sets no time limit, an agency could punish old misconduct by dismissal long after it ended. This conflicts with the principle above, so the Discipline Act's limits should apply by analogy to protect civil servants.

The Discipline Act uses ten years for every kind of sanction and does not distinguish the nature of the misconduct or the type of sanction. This does not fully match the proportionality principle, so the relevant bodies should review and revise the rules, including those in the Performance Evaluation Act.

who: Government agencies that discipline civil servants

raw.answer: The case asked what it means to "participate in a criminal organization" under Taiwan's Organized Crime Prevention Act. The court said participating means joining the organization as a member, and the crime is complete whether or not the person takes part in its activities. Whether the participation is still continuing depends on whether the person keeps taking part or keeps in contact, and prosecutors must prove it.
raw.held: Participation means joining an organization as a member, and the offense is complete on joining. Whether it continues depends on ongoing activity or contact, with prosecutors bearing the burden of proof. Earlier interpretations (including No. 68) that conflict with this are changed, and the Act's Article 18(1) transition rule does not violate the constitutional protection of personal liberty.

points.text: Criminal organizations differ from ordinary crime and endanger social order and people's rights, so they need to be prevented and eliminated; this is why the Act was made.
An organization is abstract and acts only through its members, so participation means becoming a member; the offense is complete on joining whether or not the person takes part in activities.
Whether participation is still continuing depends on whether the person keeps taking part or keeps in contact, and the prosecutor must prove this.

A member who turns themselves in before the participation is discovered, or has long had no contact and no activity, can be shown to have left, and is not treated as still participating. Limitation periods run from joining, last activity or leaving, as the case may be.

Interpretation No. 68 was issued about the now-repealed rebellion-punishment law, so it and the like interpretations are changed where they conflict with this ruling on continuing participation and burden of proof.

Article 18(1) encourages people to reform and has a limited transition period that avoids unconditional retroactive application; it does not exclude this ruling's reasoning, so it does not conflict with personal liberty protection.

who: People accused of joining criminal organizations
Members who left or turned themselves in
Members of organizations existing before the Act

raw.answer: A Taiwan high court asked whether a national security law provision requiring everyone to get permission to enter or leave the country, with criminal penalties for entering without it, is constitutional. The Constitutional Court held that, as applied to citizens who have a registered home in Taiwan, the rule breaks the proportionality principle and violates their freedom to return home at any time. That part of the law stops applying once the separate immigration rules take effect.
raw.held: The 1992-amended National Security Act Article 3(1), which required permission for all entry and exit, and its criminal penalty in Article 6, violate the proportionality principle and infringe citizens' freedom to return. They are not to be applied, to the extent inconsistent with this ruling, from when the relevant entry and exit laws take effect.

points.text: The constitutional freedom of residence and movement includes the right to enter and leave the country, and the state may not shut its citizens out of its territory.

Citizens with a home and household registration in Taiwan may return at any time without permission. Limits on entry and exit are allowed to protect national security and social order, but they must be proportionate and set by law.

The earlier wartime-period security law was tied to the situation at the time and was held not to conflict with the Constitution then. After martial law and the mobilization period ended, the legal system was expected to return to normal.

The amended Article 3(1) required permission for all entry without distinguishing citizens with a registered home in Taiwan, and punished entry without permission. This breaches proportionality and infringes the freedom to return.
Limits on people from mainland China, and on overseas Chinese nationals with no registered home in Taiwan, remain consistent with the Constitution and governed by the relevant laws.

who: Citizens with a home and household registration in Taiwan
Overseas nationals without a registered home in Taiwan
People prosecuted for entering without permission

raw.answer: When an employer owes workers unpaid wages, a fund paid by employers covers the wages, and the Bureau of Labor Insurance then seeks repayment from the employer. The question was which court system hears disputes over that repayment claim. The court decided that the ordinary (civil) courts hear them, because the claim is still a private-law debt.
raw.held: Disputes between the Bureau of Labor Insurance and an employer over the repayment claim it acquires after paying workers' wages from the fund are private-law disputes, and the ordinary courts have jurisdiction over them.

points.text: Under the Labor Standards Act, employers must pay into a wage-advance fund, which covers unpaid wages of under six months when the employer closes, liquidates or goes bankrupt, protecting workers' wages.
What the Bureau pays out from the fund is the employer's original private-law debt to the workers for wages.
The fund is paid for by employers, and paying from it is not the state giving public-law benefits from the national treasury; the Bureau acts as manager of a fund pooled by employers.
After paying, the Bureau acquires a claim against the employer that has the same scope, content and private-law nature as the workers' wage claim, and it stands in the workers' position.

The claim passes to the Bureau by operation of law, and its private nature does not change because a state body exercises it, the fund is managed by the central authority, or the fund serves a public purpose.

Fines for an employer failing to pay into the fund breach a public-law duty and go through the administrative courts, a separate matter. The court also did not address the right to sue or the procedure laws themselves.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Labor Standards Act is unconstitutional because it does not bar a worker's right to claim retirement pay from being transferred, offset, seized or pledged as security, unlike the rule for civil servants. The court decided that the difference is not unconstitutional. It found that the law-makers chose this difference within their freedom to shape the law, and that it does not breach the equality principle in Article 7.
raw.held: The Labor Standards Act does not say, as the civil servants' retirement rules do, that the right to claim retirement pay cannot be seized, transferred or pledged. This is a matter for the legislature's freedom to design the law and does not violate the constitutional equality principle (Article 7).

points.text: Equality under Article 7 means real equality in legal position, not rigid formal sameness, so the legislature may treat things differently when their nature differs, for reasonable reasons.

A worker's right to claim retirement pay is a private-law claim protected as property. Whether to bar its transfer, offset, seizure or pledge limits the property rights of workers, employers and other creditors. The legislature must therefore weigh these interests in light of social and economic conditions.

Civil servants and workers differ in the nature of their work and in their rights and duties. Civil servants have a public-law relationship with the state, while employment is a private contract relationship. So the state's methods of protecting their retirement are not the same.
Whether the differences breach equality must be judged by looking at all protective measures as a whole, not at a single feature.

The civil servants' rule serves the constitutional aim of protecting their retirement. The legislature weighed the conflicting interests differently for workers and chose differently. That does not show workers' retirement is under-protected or that Article 153 or Article 7 is violated.

The later Labor Pension Act bars transfer, seizure, offset and pledge of pension claims, a different choice reflecting current conditions. Whether to add such a rule to the Labor Standards Act's existing system remains for the legislature.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the rules for charging a vehicle fuel usage fee, including who pays and how the fee is calculated, were unconstitutional. The court decided they were not: the Highway Act gave clear authority for the fee, and the charging rules did not violate the principles of legal reservation, equality or proportionality. It also found the fee is not double taxation together with the vehicle license tax.
raw.held: The Highway Act's fuel fee provision and the 1997 fee collection measures (Articles 2 and 3) stay within the authority granted by law and do not violate the Constitution's equality or proportionality principles. The fee and the vehicle license tax do not amount to double taxation.

points.text: Non-tax money duties imposed for a public purpose affect property rights, so the purpose, who pays and the amount must be set by law or by a clear, specific delegation of authority.
The Highway Act sets the purpose, the payers and the maximum rate, and clearly delegates the collection method and distribution to the authorities, so the delegation is sufficiently clear.

Charging vehicle owners and estimating fuel use from engine displacement, mileage and efficiency stays within the Act's delegation, because the fee funds highway needs and need not track actual fuel use, given collection cost and technical choices.

Charging vehicle owners is not arbitrary: it serves a major public interest, owners benefit from the highways, and the money is used for road upkeep. Using one rate for all gasoline grades is reasonable too.

The calculation method is reasonably related to the purpose: larger engines tend to burn more fuel and may burden roads more, commercial vehicles use more, and the lower diesel rate rests on transport and industrial policy. So it is proportionate.
The vehicle license tax serves general government revenue while the fuel fee funds road upkeep, so their nature and purpose differ and there is no double taxation.

who: Drivers of gasoline and diesel vehicles

raw.answer: The case asked whether a regulation implementing the law on restoring rights lost during the martial law period was unconstitutional because it defined "civil servants" (公務人員) as civilian staff only, leaving out military personnel. The court decided the definition is not unconstitutional. It said the exclusion rests on real differences between the two groups and stays within what the parent law allowed.
raw.held: The regulation defining "civil servants" as salaried civilian staff, which excludes military personnel, does not violate the equality principle, does not exceed the parent law's authorization, and does not conflict with the Constitution. Whether qualifications to serve in military posts should be restored is left to the legislature.

points.text: Under the Constitution and the civil service appointment law, a "civil servant" is someone who gained appointment qualification through legal examination and screening and holds a titled post and rank in a statutory agency.

Laws that use the term "civil servant" (pay, protection, promotion, evaluation, retirement, pensions) do not apply to military personnel, so in current law the term means career civilian officials only.

In the restoration law, "civil servant" sits alongside education personnel and public office holders, so its scope is limited to civilian staff. This differs from the clause on pensions and insurance, which is not limited to civilians.

Military personnel fight or do defense-related work tied to national security, and their training, age limits for rank, promotion conditions and duty of obedience differ from civilians. The exclusion therefore reflects real differences and does not breach equality.
Because of this, the regulation stays within the parent law's authorization and does not conflict with the Constitution.
Whether qualifications for military posts should be restored is for the legislature to decide.

who: People who lost rights during martial law

raw.answer: The case asked whether an implementing rule and a Ministry of Finance letter could deny the estate and gift tax exemption to farmland that had been officially zoned for non-farm use but was still being farmed. The court held they could not, because they added limits that the statute does not contain. It ruled the rule and the letter violate the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on statute, and they may no longer be applied.
raw.held: The rule in the Agricultural Development Act's implementing regulations and the Ministry of Finance letter both added limits not found in the law, and so violate the constitutional principle of taxation by statute and the protection of property. They may no longer be applied to land zoned for non-farm use but still farmed within its permitted period.

points.text: Under the constitution, taxpayers' duties and tax relief must be set by statute, and implementing rules may only cover details; they cannot add to or reduce the statute's terms or add limits on people's rights.
The Act's exemption statute was not amended, yet the later administrative rules and letters effectively changed the tax burden, which is hard to square with taxation by statute.

The Act defines agricultural land by how it is used and does not require it to be zoned for farming. Under the Land Act, land zoned for another use may still be used as before until the stated deadline, so such land can still count.
If the Ministry of Finance thought the exemption too broad, it had to seek amendment of the Act itself, not narrow it through implementing rules or interpretive directives.

The rule and the letter narrowed the Act's definition of agricultural land by decree, even if this served the aim of encouraging agriculture, so they added limits the law lacks and conflict with property protection and the legal-reservation principle.
The ruling applies only to the laws in force when the underlying events occurred, not to the later 2000 amendments.

who: Owners of farmland zoned for non-farm use but still farmed

raw.answer: More than one-third of legislators asked the Constitutional Court to rule that Article 8 of the Household Registration Act may violate the constitution. It requires fingerprinting to get a national ID card. They also asked the court to suspend the rule while it decided. The court agreed to suspend paragraphs 2 and 3 of the article, but refused to suspend paragraph 1.
raw.held: Article 8, paragraphs 2 and 3, and the related rules requiring fingerprints to get or replace the new ID card, are suspended until the main ruling is issued, or at most six months. The request to suspend paragraph 1 is rejected.

points.text: The court can issue temporary orders to keep its eventual ruling effective. It can do so when serious, hard-to-undo harm to basic rights or public interests is urgent, no other means can prevent it, and the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks.
The fingerprint rules raise major constitutional questions, including whether fingerprints can be required for ID cards and whether forced fingerprint recording infringes basic rights.

From 1 July 2005 people would have to give fingerprints to get the new ID card, so the possible harm was widespread and urgent with no other way to prevent it. The long replacement period does not remove the urgency.
If the rules were later found unconstitutional, recorded fingerprints could cause harm that is hard to undo, and destroying the files would waste large administrative resources.

Suspending the rules mostly continues the current situation and would not seriously hinder household registration or daily life for existing card holders. Extra administrative cost is smaller than the harm to rights.

The request about paragraph 1 was rejected: it only sets a general age rule for the duty and right to get an ID card, and the applicants did not show how it harms protected rights. Authorities must still issue old-style cards or other interim measures.

who: People who must or may apply for or replace a national ID card from 1 July 2005
People who already hold ID cards

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Arbitration Act is unconstitutional because it does not list contradictory reasoning in an arbitral award as a ground for suing to set the award aside. The court held that this omission is constitutional. It found that it is a design choice within the legislature's freedom that fits arbitration's nature and does not conflict with the constitutional right to bring a lawsuit.
raw.held: The Arbitration Act (as amended on 24 June 1998) lets parties sue to set aside an award that lacks required reasons but not one with contradictory reasons. This does not exceed the legislature's freedom to shape the law and does not violate Article 16 of the Constitution on the right to sue.

points.text: The right to sue under Article 16 guarantees legal procedures and fair trials, but the legislature may set reasonable procedures and requirements, taking into account out-of-court ways of settling disputes.

People are the holders of private-law rights and may choose litigation or a lawful non-court process. Arbitration, based on party agreement and freedom of contract, is a self-determined way to resolve private disputes that the Constitution permits.

The state should assist and supervise arbitration, but it is common internationally to limit by law the grounds for setting aside awards. The UNCITRAL Model Law's grounds mostly concern serious procedural defects, so courts do not re-examine the substance of awards and arbitration stays autonomous and fast.

The Act allows suits over awards that lack required reasons, for example, but a court can tell whether reasons are missing from the award and the arbitration documents. Judging contradictory reasoning would require re-examining the facts and the soundness of the reasons, which is different.

Leaving out contradictory reasons reflects arbitration's character and international practice. It is necessary for arbitration's healthy development, falls within the legislature's freedom, and does not conflict with Article 16.

who: Parties seeking to set aside arbitral awards

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Taiwan provincial rule on registering the end of farmland leases was unconstitutional. The rule requires a landlord who ends a lease for unpaid rent to submit certain documents, including a notice demanding the overdue rent. The court held the rule is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: The rule requiring landlords to submit documents such as a rent-demand notice when registering a lease termination for unpaid rent does not exceed the authority the law gave and does not conflict with the Constitution. The challenge to other articles of the registration rules was not accepted for review.

points.text: The registration rules were issued under authority given by the farmland rent reduction law, and requiring applicants to submit supporting documents is a detailed, technical, secondary matter that the authorized agency may fill in.
The farmland rent reduction law says matters it does not cover follow other laws, which include the Civil Code's rules on leases.
Under the Civil Code, a landlord must first set a deadline and demand overdue rent before ending a lease, which protects tenants, and this also applies to ending farmland leases for unpaid rent.
So requiring a rent-demand notice matches the law and adds no restriction the law does not contain.
The challenge to other articles of the registration rules was dismissed because it disputed how the court applied the law and did not specifically show how the rules conflicted with the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Equalization of Land Rights Act is unconstitutional. The rule makes a landowner pay the tenant farmer one third of the compensation, after land value increment tax, when rented farmland is expropriated. The court held that the rule does not violate the landowner's property rights, but said it should be reviewed and revised quickly. It also declined to hear the part of the request that attacked a final court judgment.
raw.held: The rule that the landowner pays the tenant one third of the compensation, after land value increment tax, with the authority deducting it and handing it over, does not infringe the landowner's property rights. The court added that the rule should be reviewed and revised promptly to fit the Constitution.

points.text: Property is protected by the Constitution. When the state expropriates land, it must give reasonable compensation that matches the loss, to both the owner and other rights holders. The legislature has some freedom to choose how to compensate.

A tenant farmer's lease is a constitutionally protected property right, and the state must also compensate the tenant when expropriation ends it. Because of rent caps, limits on ending leases, and the lease binding a buyer, the lease works like a burden on the land.

Compensation for rented and unrented farmland is calculated on the same basis. So the compensation for rented land in effect covers both the owner's remaining value in the land and the value of the lease burden on it.

The one-third figure was drawn from earlier investment-incentive rules and from custom between owners and tenants. It was an estimate of the lease's value, and the authority pays the tenant from the owner's compensation.

The provision only sets the procedure and the split of the compensation. It fits the protection of property and of farmers and the principle that compensation matches loss. It stays within the legislature's freedom, so it does not harm the owner's property rights.

Because the economy and industry have changed, the court said the rule based on the lease as a burden on the land should be reviewed and revised quickly. Separately, the court cannot review a final judgment itself or a court's reading of a law. So that part of the request was not accepted.

who: Legislature and the authorities that pay compensation

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance notice that suspended income tax on securities trading gains for individuals selling up to NT$10 million of listed stock a year was unconstitutional. The court decided it was not. It found the notice rested on authority given by a statute and was a reasonable difference in treatment.
raw.held: The notice's rule suspending tax on stock trading gains (for individuals selling no more than NT$10 million a year, from 1989 to 1990, with trading losses not deductible) does not conflict with the constitutional requirement that taxes be set by law, nor with the equality principle.

points.text: The state may impose or reduce taxes under conditions set by law, or by orders that a law specifically and clearly authorizes, if there is a proper reason for reasonable differences. This does not breach tax-by-law or equality.

The Statute for Investment Encouragement, Article 27, let the Executive Yuan suspend tax on securities trading gains of people who do not trade securities as a profession, based on economic needs and market conditions. The notice was issued on that authority.
The notice gives a limited preference to individuals' securities gains, which matches the statute's purpose of limiting relief to non-professional traders. So it does not conflict with Article 19.
Equality under Article 7 means real equality in legal standing, not rigid formal equality. Special tax relief for a defined group, for the public interest and with proper reason, is not forbidden.

Suspending tax only for trades up to a set amount was a reasonable difference. The agency, acting on legal authorization, weighed the stage of economic development and actual market conditions with professional judgment.

who: Ministry of Finance and the Executive Yuan

raw.answer: The case asked whether the National Health Insurance Act's requirement that local governments subsidize insurance premiums is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not unconstitutional, because the premium subsidy is a share of the insurance payment and not an administrative cost, and central government may in this way require local governments to share it. The court also said local governments must be given a real voice when such laws are drafted.
raw.held: Article 27 of the National Health Insurance Act, which makes local governments subsidize part of insured people's premiums, does not violate the Constitution. The subsidy percentages are left to the legislature's discretion unless clearly improper, but local governments must be fully involved in making such laws.

points.text: The duty to promote national health insurance falls on both central and local government, and local governments' own duties to look after residents' welfare can partly be met through the insurance scheme.

The Act's administrative costs must be paid by the central government, but the local subsidy under Article 27 is not an administrative cost; it is the payment that secures coverage for the insured, alongside employer and central contributions.

Local governments have constitutionally protected financial autonomy, but the central government may use legislation to make them share premium subsidies as long as the core of that autonomy is not harmed.

Harming the core means hollowing out local autonomy, such as the center drawing up local budgets or making locals pay for unrelated matters like foreign affairs or defense. Sharing costs where duties overlap or where it fits the nature of the matter is not such harm.

The Constitution does not set how financial responsibility is divided between center and localities. The Act on Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures does not bar a special rule, and Article 27 is such a special rule.

The subsidy percentages for each type of insured person are for the legislature to decide, and are unconstitutional only if clearly improper. Local governments must be consulted and heard when such laws are drafted and amended.

who: People insured under national health insurance
